title: How long? (Psalm 13)
hook: injustice cries out, and God hears the cry

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mother in Ramah who would not be comforted, and hope spoken beside her tears. Your line was rachel weeping.

Two words and a question mark. They're on protest signs and in hospital waiting rooms. A tenant says them about the landlord who won't fix the heat. A family says them about a trial that keeps getting postponed. A child says them in the back seat, and a whole people says them across generations. How long? It sounds like impatience. In the Bible it's something else: a prayer, and a cry about what is wrong. A short psalm asks it again and again, and the Bible keeps answering that the cry is heard.

Back on day one hundred five, this psalm taught that complaint is a prayer too, and not long ago its first line came up as an argument with God. Today, listen for verse two, where a third figure enters, the enemy: "How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?" Someone is winning who shouldn't be. That turns how long from a sigh into a cry about injustice. And the Bible says that kind of cry is heard. From the burning bush, God says in Exodus: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows." Seen, heard, known, and every word points at people worked by taskmasters. The prophet Habakkuk opens with the same complaint, about violence and judgment gone crooked: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" And in Revelation, the souls of those slain for the word of God cry from under the altar: "How long, O Lord, holy and true?" From the psalms to the last book, the question is never thrown out. Then Psalm thirteen ends in a strange place. Nothing outside has changed yet. But the voice says, "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." The cry and the trust come from the same mouth. How long is one of the ways people pray about what's wrong, and keep praying.
screen: `HOW LONG, O LORD, HOLY AND TRUE?`
`BUT I HAVE TRUSTED IN THY MERCY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one wrong that has gone on too long, far away or on your own street: someone underpaid, someone unheard, someone waiting for a hearing that never comes, and name it plainly. If you pray, bring it to God in the psalm's own words, how long, O Lord; if you don't, just hold it in the open, without looking away.
How long? The cry of Psalm thirteen, spoken straight to God when wrong is winning, and kept in scripture as a prayer.
Your line: how long, o lord? In the Bible, that cry is heard, and kept. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians pray the lament psalms, including Psalm 13, in worship and in private, and churches and Christian groups bring that cry into action through advocacy, legal aid, protest and care for people who are being wronged.

fork.setup: you're the voice of Psalm 13. God seems to have forgotten you, and your enemy is winning. what do you do?
options: stay silent, because questioning God is not allowed.
ask God straight out, how long?, and then speak your trust.
give up on God and stop praying.
fork.reveal: the psalm does both: it asks how long again and again, then says, but I have trusted in thy mercy. the question and the trust share one short psalm.

chat.says: Isn't asking God 'how long?' just being impatient with him?
options: In Psalm 13 it's a prayer, a cry about wrong winning, and the psalm ends in trust.
Yes. The psalm asks it once, then takes it back and apologizes to God.
Yes. Only Psalm 13 asks it; the rest of the Bible never repeats the question.
chat.meaning: Psalm 13 asks how long while an enemy is winning, and still ends, I have trusted in thy mercy. Habakkuk and Revelation ask it too.

burning bush.meaning: the bush from which God speaks in Exodus

taskmasters.meaning: overseers who drove the Israelites to work in Egypt

Habakkuk.meaning: a prophet whose book opens with how long

Revelation.meaning: the Bible's last book, full of visions
